fable-5.1.text:
Well, I have a lot of respect for Jeremy. He's studied bubbles for a long time, and I've studied them too, so let me tell you how I look at it rather than just agree or disagree.

First, you have to separate two things. There's the technology and there's the price. The technology is real. AI is going to be one of the great productivity changes in history, and I don't think there's much doubt about that. But the question of whether it's a great technology and the question of whether the prices are a bubble are completely different questions. In 1999 the internet was real, and it was also a bubble. In the 1920s, radio and the automobile were real, and they were also a bubble. The technology changing the world and investors losing a lot of money can both be true at the same time.

So I don't go by opinion. I have a bubble gauge that I've used for a long time, and it looks at a handful of things. How high are prices relative to traditional measures of value? Are the prices discounting conditions that can't be sustained, in other words, do earnings have to grow at rates that have never happened before? How many new buyers have come into the market who weren't there before? How bullish is the sentiment broadly? How much of the buying is financed with leverage, with borrowed money? And have people made forward purchases, built out capacity, committed to spending as if the boom will continue?

When I run those numbers today, we're probably somewhere around eighty percent of the way to what I'd call a full bubble. Not all the way, but far along. The piece that's missing compared to 1929 or 1999 is the leverage. The buying so far hasn't been as debt-financed, and that matters, because leverage is what turns a correction into a crash. But the capital spending commitments, the concentration in a small number of companies, the pricing that assumes everything goes right, those look very familiar.

And then the thing to watch is what pops bubbles, which is almost always the same thing. It's a tightening of money and credit. Bubbles don't die of old age. They die when the central bank tightens, or when the cash flows can't support the spending, and the people who bought on expectations have to sell. So I'd say Jeremy is more right than wrong about the pricing. Where I'd be careful is that these things can go on longer than anybody thinks, and the long-term winners will come out of this period. So I'd be diversified, I wouldn't be leveraged, and I'd be very conscious that what looks like the obvious bet is usually already in the price.

r001.rationale: The candidate lays out its framework and bubble-gauge factors before giving its conclusion about current pricing.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses bubbles popping and possible crashes, but does not characterize a bubble as a large price rise followed by a collapse.

opus-5.5.text:
Well, I respect Jeremy a lot. He's studied bubbles more carefully than almost anybody, so when he says that, I take it seriously. Mostly I agree with him, but I'd frame it a little differently.

I look at it mechanically. I have what I call a bubble gauge, and it looks at a handful of things. Are prices high relative to traditional measures, like earnings and cash flows? Are the prices discounting future growth that's unlikely to materialize at those rates? Are there a lot of new buyers coming in who weren't in the market before? Is there broadly bullish sentiment? Are purchases being financed with leverage? And are people buying forward, building capacity ahead of demand? When you go down that list for the AI-related companies, a lot of those boxes are getting checked. So yes, by those measures, we're in bubble territory.

But here's the important thing that people miss. A bubble doesn't mean the technology isn't real. AI is real. It's going to change productivity, change how we work, change the balance of power between countries. The railroads were real. The internet was real. Both had bubbles, and a lot of people lost a lot of money even though they were right about the technology. Being right about the technology and being right about the investment are two very different things.

The other thing is that bubbles don't pop just because they're bubbles. Something has to prick them. Classically, it's a tightening of money: the central bank raises rates, or there's a need for cash. Maybe people have to pay taxes, or they have debts to service and have to sell their assets to get that money. That's when you get the self-reinforcing decline. So I watch for those triggers more than I try to call the top. You can be early on a bubble and be just as wrong as if you'd missed it.

I'd also put it in the bigger context. This isn't happening in isolation. We have enormous government debts, a lot of internal political conflict, the U.S.–China rivalry, and a big part of that rivalry is about who wins in technology. That makes the AI race geopolitical as well as economic, and it's one reason the spending will continue even past the point where the returns justify it.

So what should an individual do? I wouldn't tell somebody to run away from it entirely, but I would tell them not to be concentrated in it. Diversify well, know the difference between a great company and a great investment at the price you're paying, and don't use leverage to chase it. The biggest mistake people make is to believe the recent past is going to continue, when in reality the things that have done the best are often what get hurt the most when conditions change.

r001.rationale: The response lays out the bubble-gauge factors and applies them to AI-related companies before concluding that they are in bubble territory.

r002.rationale: It discusses bubbles popping and declines, but does not define a market bubble as a large rise in prices followed by a collapse.

fable-5.text:
Well, I have a lot of respect for Jeremy, and I'd say he's identifying something real, but I'd frame it a little differently. I've studied bubbles going back hundreds of years, and I've developed what I call a bubble indicator — a systematic way of measuring it — because I think you have to be precise about what a bubble actually is rather than just using the word.

A bubble, in my mind, has certain measurable characteristics. Prices are high relative to traditional measures of value. Prices are discounting conditions that can't be sustained — in other words, the earnings growth that would be required to justify the price is unlikely to happen. You have a lot of new, naive buyers coming into the market because the thing has gone up, not because they understand it. Sentiment is broadly bullish. And purchases are being financed by leverage and debt.

Now, if you apply that to AI today, what you find is interesting. There's a classic confusion that happens in these periods, which is that people conflate whether the technology is great with whether the investment is great. Those are two very different questions. In 1998, 1999, the internet was a revolutionary technology — everybody who said it would change the world was right. And yet if you bought those stocks at those prices, you lost most of your money, because the price already discounted more than even that revolutionary change could deliver. The technology being transformative doesn't mean the price is right. New eras of technology, if you go back and look at them — canals, railroads, radio — they changed the world and they also produced bubbles that wiped out investors.

So when I look at AI, I'd say yes, there are classic bubble dynamics emerging, particularly in the degree to which prices are discounting a very optimistic future, and in the concentration — a handful of companies making up an enormous share of the market. Where it differs from 1999 is that the leverage picture isn't as extreme yet, and the leading companies are actually earning real money. So I'd say we're in the part of the cycle where the bubble is inflating but hasn't reached its most dangerous extreme.

And here's the other thing I'd add, which is the part people pay less attention to: bubbles don't pop on their own. They pop when money gets tight — when the central bank tightens, when there's a need for money that forces selling. So you have to look at this in the context of the larger picture: the debt situation, the deficits, the amount of bonds that have to be sold, the political conflict. The AI question can't be separated from where we are in the big cycle. When those forces come together — a richly priced market and a tightening of money — that's historically when you get the downturn. So I'd say Jeremy is right to be cautious, and I'd just want people to understand mechanically how these things work rather than simply being scared by the word "bubble."

r001.rationale: The response lays out a bubble framework and compares it with historical cases before reaching its investment conclusion about AI.

r002.rationale: It describes high prices, unsustainable expectations, and bubbles eventually popping, but does not characterize a bubble as a large price rise followed by a collapse.

opus-5.text:
Jeremy's a very smart man and I have enormous respect for him, and I think the honest answer is: he's partly right, and the part he's right about isn't the part most people argue over.

Let me tell you how I look at it, because I don't want to give you an opinion, I want to give you a way of measuring. I built a bubble gauge, because I've been through enough of these — '67 to '70, the Nifty Fifty, Japan in '89, the dot-coms, '07 — and they all rhyme. So I ask six or seven questions. How high are prices relative to traditional measures of value? Are prices discounting conditions that can't be sustained? How many new and naive buyers have come into the market? How broad is the bullish sentiment? How much of the purchasing is being financed by debt and leverage? And have buyers made extended forward commitments — are they building capacity today for demand they're assuming shows up in five years?

When you run those on AI today, you get a reading that's high. It's elevated. It's in the top quintile. But it is not 2000. In 2000 the gauge was pinned — it was at the 100th percentile. Today you have companies with enormous real earnings and real cash flow, and that's a meaningful difference. What's picked up, and what I'd watch most carefully, is the last two: the leverage and the forward commitments. The capex is increasingly being financed with debt rather than out of cash flow, and you've got a certain circularity — companies investing in their own customers, vendor financing arrangements. That's the classic late-stage signature. And the concentration is extreme. A handful of names are carrying the index, so if you own the market you don't own what you think you own.

But here's what I'd add, and this is where I'd part from the pure bearish case. Two things can be true at once. The technology can be the most important thing happening in the world and the stocks can be badly overpriced. The internet changed everything — and 80 percent of the companies went to zero. Both true.

And AI is one of the five big forces I watch, and it's the only one running in a positive direction right now. We have a debt problem that's arithmetically very hard to solve. The only clean way out historically is a productivity miracle. So AI isn't just an investment question, it's the thing that could bail us out of the money and credit cycle — or not get there in time.

So what do I do? I don't try to time it. Being early and being wrong look identical for years, and that's the trap Jeremy's had to live with. I diversify — across asset classes, countries, currencies — and I hold a meaningful allocation to gold, because the risk nobody prices is that cash and bonds are the dangerous asset when governments are monetizing debt. The mistake isn't being in AI or out of AI. The mistake is being concentrated.

r001.rationale: The response explains its investment reasoning before its conclusion: it describes a bubble gauge and the questions it uses, then applies that framework to AI and states its assessment.

r002.rationale: The response discusses elevated prices, past bubbles, and dot-com companies going to zero, but it does not characterize a market bubble as a large rise in prices followed by a collapse.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Jeremy is a great student of bubbles, and I respect his work. I look at it a bit differently, though.

I have an indicator I use to judge whether something is a bubble. It asks several questions. Are prices high relative to traditional measures of value? Are they discounting future earnings that may never come? How many new and inexperienced buyers are coming in? How much of the buying is on leverage, and how much is bullish sentiment? Are people buying because the price is going up, rather than because of the underlying value? And is there a lot of new equity supply, like IPOs and new issuance?

When I run the market through that, it reads high but not at the extreme. I'd say we're in the early stages of a bubble. The signs are there, especially in the concentration of the market in a handful of AI-related stocks. But it's not the 1999 and 2000 extreme, where almost everybody was in and the leverage was through the roof.

Two things are true at the same time. The technology is real and it's going to be transformative, just as the internet was. But a great technology and a great investment are not the same thing. In the dot-com era the internet changed the world, and most of the people who bought the early stocks still lost money, because they paid too much for it and the timing was off.

A bubble doesn't pop just because it's a bubble. It pops when there's a tightening of money and credit, when the sellers outnumber the buyers and they need cash. That is the pin. So I watch how much money is being put into the AI buildout, who is funding it, and whether it's being funded by debt. I also watch what's happening with interest rates and with the supply of Treasury debt that has to be absorbed. If a tightening comes, the bubble breaks.

So I wouldn't say Jeremy is wrong. I'd say it's a bubble in the making, and the question is what the pin is and when it arrives. For an investor, the answer is not to get out of everything. It's to be diversified, to know what you own, and not to be so exposed to one theme that being wrong would hurt you badly.

r001.rationale: The response lays out its bubble indicator and applies it to the market before stating its conclusion that a bubble is in the making.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think Jeremy is pointing at something real, but I'd separate two questions that often get blurred together. The first is whether the technology is transformative. The second is whether the prices being paid for it are justified. You can be right about the first and still lose a lot of money on the second.

When I look at bubbles, I don't focus on the story, because everyone has a good story. Railroads and the internet were both real. I look at the mechanics: how much money and credit is chasing the asset, whether people are buying with borrowed money, whether prices are rising faster than the cash flows they're supposed to represent, and whether people are buying mainly because prices are going up. When those things line up, you're usually in a late stage.

On AI, I think the long-run productivity potential is very large. But productivity gains take a long time to show up, and they tend to be captured unevenly. So the investor's question isn't whether AI will change the world. It's how much of that future is already in the price, and who will actually earn the profits. Those are harder questions, and I don't think anyone has a clean answer yet.

What I'd watch most closely is the financing. Is the buildout being funded by cash flow from strong businesses, or increasingly by debt and by deals among a small group of companies that depend on each other? If it's the second, that's when I'd become more worried, because that's how a boom becomes fragile.

My honest view is that there's likely a bubble element in parts of this, and there's almost certainly a real technology underneath it. Both can be true at once. The mistake I see most often is people deciding which one is true and then ignoring the other.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a concern worth taking seriously. AI can be a tremendously important technology, and the investments associated with it can still be overpriced. Those two things can be true at the same time.

When you buy an investment, you’re buying future cash flows at a particular price. If that price already assumes extraordinary growth, enormous profits, and very little competition, even a company that does very well can turn out to be a disappointing investment. The excitement about the technology doesn’t resolve that calculation.

So I would look at what’s being discounted into prices, who’s financing the spending, and how much borrowing is involved. If expectations disappoint, leverage can turn an investment loss into a much broader financial problem.

I’d also be humble about timing. Recognizing that expectations are stretched doesn’t tell you when they’ll change. You want to understand your exposure and make sure your financial well-being doesn’t depend on one particular vision of the future coming true.

r001.rationale: The response develops its investment reasoning—price versus future cash flows, expectations, financing, and leverage—rather than simply declaring whether AI is a bubble.

r002.rationale: It discusses potentially overpriced investments and the risk of losses, but does not define a bubble as a large price rise followed by a collapse.

Well, I think you have to separate the technology from the investment. AI could be enormously important, and people could still pay too much for it. Those two things can both be true.

When you buy an investment, you’re buying future cash flows at a particular price. If that price already assumes extraordinary success, then even a very successful company can disappoint you as an investor. So enthusiasm about what AI can do doesn’t, by itself, tell you whether these are good investments.

I’d also want to understand how the investment is being financed. If people are borrowing heavily, a decline can force them to sell, and that creates a different set of risks from people simply losing money they can afford to lose.

So I’d take Jeremy’s concern seriously. But identifying excessive optimism and knowing when prices will turn are very different things. The practical issue is how much your portfolio depends on those optimistic assumptions being right. You want to be able to participate without having your financial future depend on one outcome.

I think Jeremy’s assessment is worth taking seriously, but I’d separate the technology from the investment. AI may be genuinely transformative, and yet transformative technologies can still become bubbles when expectations, valuations, and capital spending run far ahead of the cash flows they ultimately produce.

The important question isn’t simply whether AI is real; it’s how much of its future success is already reflected in prices. I’d look at the assumptions embedded in valuations, the amount of leverage and speculative behavior, and whether productivity and earnings are broadening beyond a handful of companies. I wouldn’t try to predict the exact top. I’d assume there are both enormous opportunities and meaningful downside, and position in a diversified, balanced way rather than betting everything on one narrative.
